content.title: 10 Long-term sequelae of pulmonary embolism
content.summary: Patency of the pulmonary arterial bed is restored in the majority of PE survivors within the first few months; routine follow-up CTPA is not needed for such patients. In some patients thrombi become persistent and organized and may rarely result in CTEPH, a potentially life‑threatening obstructing vasculopathy. Follow-up after PE should (i) provide appropriate care (rehabilitation, treatment of comorbidity, education, risk factor modification) for patients with persisting symptoms and (ii) ensure early detection of CTEPH for further diagnostic workup and treatment.
recommendations: No routine follow-up CTPA imaging is needed in patients whose pulmonary arterial bed is restored after PE.
Efficient follow-up strategy should focus on rehabilitation, treatment of comorbidity, behavioural education, modification of risk factors, and early detection/referral for CTEPH when indicated.
content.section_10.1_heading: Persisting symptoms and functional limitation after pulmonary embolism
section_10.1_key_points: Cohort studies over the past decade report persisting or deteriorating dyspnoea and poor physical performance frequently present 6 months to 3 years after an acute PE episode.
Proportion of patients reporting worse health status at 6 months vs time of PE diagnosis varies widely (approximately 20% to 75%).

Identified baseline predictors of exertional dyspnoea at long-term follow-up after PE include: advanced age; cardiac or pulmonary comorbidity; higher body mass index; history of smoking; higher systolic pulmonary arterial pressure (PAP) and right ventricular (RV) dysfunction at diagnosis; and residual pulmonary vascular obstruction at discharge.
content.cohort_study_findings: A prospective cohort study of 100 patients at five Canadian hospitals (2010–2013) followed for 1 year found up to 47% of patients had reduced maximal aerobic capacity (peak oxygen consumption <80% of predicted on cardiopulmonary exercise testing), associated with significantly worse generic health-related outcomes.
